sections.overview: The upland goose is a South American sheldgoose of open Patagonian country and the Falkland Islands. It is one of several related Chloephaga geese, including the ruddy-headed goose C. rubidiceps and the ash-headed goose C. poliocephala.
sections.identification: The sexes look strikingly different: males are largely white with bold black barring on some plumage, while females are brown and barred, with yellow legs. Its black bill and generally large, goose-like build help separate it from smaller, more uniformly coloured waterfowl.
sections.habitat: It uses open grasslands, steppe and damp meadows, often near lakes, rivers or marshy ground. On the continent it breeds in southern Chile and Argentina, with seasonal movements northward; island populations occur in the Falklands.
sections.diet: It is primarily a grazer, feeding on grasses and other soft vegetation, including seeds.
sections.behavior: It forms large flocks, but breeding pairs defend a territory. It is rarely seen in water except when tending young.
sections.reproduction: It nests on the ground in grassland, often near wetlands, lining the nest with down. The female incubates a clutch while the male guards the pair’s territory; goslings leave the nest soon after hatching and are led by their parents.
sections.ecology: By grazing native grassland and crop pasture, it affects forage plants and can come into conflict with ranching. The ruddy-headed goose occurs in the same broad region but is a distinct close relative, so records should not be conflated.
sections.conservation: Chile classified the species as Vulnerable in its 2022 national assessment; this country-level category does not represent a global assessment.
